enrichment.short_title: Judicial review after failed immigration statutory review
key_facts: Two asylum claimants sought judicial review of Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusals of permission to appeal after High Court judges had rejected statutory review under section 101(3) of the 2002 Act.
The government introduced statutory review to replace judicial review in IAT permission cases, with paper-only review and a final High Court decision.
Claimants argued that judicial review jurisdiction survived and that Article 6 and Article 14 ECHR were breached.
Collins J granted permission in the second claim and heard both together.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of IAT refusal of permission to appeal following unsuccessful statutory review under section 101(3).
enrichment.outcome: Both claims dismissed; judicial review jurisdiction survives but is an exceptional remedy of last resort after statutory review, and these claims were an abuse of process.
enrichment.ratio: Section 101 of the 2002 Act does not oust judicial review by clear words, but where statutory review exists Parliament intended it to replace judicial review; a claim re-arguing grounds already rejected in statutory review is an abuse unless there are very exceptional circumstances such as fraud or bias.
legal_issues: Whether section 101 ousts judicial review of IAT permission decisions
Whether statutory review is a satisfactory alternative remedy barring judicial review
Whether refusal of judicial review breaches Articles 6 and 14 ECHR
Whether failed statutory review creates an estoppel or abuse of process

enrichment.short_title: Privacy of section 68 arbitration challenge judgments
key_facts: Moscow sought publication of Cooke J's judgment dismissing Bankers Trust and IIB applications under section 68 of the 1996 Act arising from a confidential UNCITRAL arbitration.
The section 68 hearing was held in private under CPR 62.10(3)(b), but a Lawtel summary was briefly published online.
The dispute concerned a Credit Agreement between Moscow, Bankers Trust and IIB involving politically and commercially sensitive material.
Cooke J refused publication of the full judgment but also prohibited publication of the neutral Lawtel summary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court order refusing publication of a section 68 judgment and Lawtel summary.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed in relation to the full judgment but allowed in relation to the Lawtel summary, which may be published generally; Moscow to pay 85% of Bankers Trust's appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 62.10 establishes a starting point of privacy for section 68 hearings, but publication of a reasoned judgment raises distinct considerations; where a judgment contains highly confidential factual material and the successful party has no good reason for publication, privacy may be justified, yet a factually neutral summary already in the public domain should not be suppressed.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal: new country guidance not before tribunal
key_facts: Mr Lusala, a Congolese national of mixed Hutu and Bakongo ethnicity, claimed asylum based on ethnicity and objection to military service.
An adjudicator rejected the claim and the IAT refused permission to appeal on 9 June 2003.
On appeal, Lusala relied on later UKIAT country guidance in M (DR Congo) and a UNHCR report cited there.
That material had not been before the IAT when it decided his case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal, with permission, against an IAT refusal of permission to appeal on a point of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal to the Court of Appeal is on a point of law arising from the tribunal's decision; material that was not before the tribunal cannot found an error of law, and the Polat concession does not assist where the relevant evidence was never submitted to the tribunal.

enrichment.short_title: Constructive trust over secret commissions from refurbishment contracts
key_facts: Mr Khalid, an employee and adviser to Sheikh Mohammed of Qatar, received about £1.8 million in secret 10% commissions from Solland companies on luxury property refurbishment contracts worth over £20 million.
Commissions were built into contract prices and paid through Interiors and later through offshore company International.
Proceedings against the Sollands settled; Mr Khalid did not attend trial and default judgments were entered against his nominees.
The claimants sought restitution, constructive trust, and damages for deceit and conspiracy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial following settlement with other defendants, determining liability and remedies against the absent commission recipient.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimants against Mr Khalid, including a proprietary constructive trust over the secret commissions and traceable proceeds.
enrichment.ratio: A fiduciary who receives secret commissions is accountable on constructive trust under AG for Hong Kong v Reid rather than merely as a debtor under Lister v Stubbs, especially where the bribe was built into the price paid by the principal and extracted from the principal's own money.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Khalid owed fiduciary duties to the claimants as agent or employee
Whether AG for Hong Kong v Reid displaces Lister & Co v Stubbs

enrichment.short_title: Travel agent liability for cancelled Balkan airline tickets

statutes_considered.title: Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982

key_facts: Payless Travel procured Balkan Bulgarian Airlines tickets for Baba Krupa Holidays passengers flying to Dubai on 23 March 2002.
Balkan cancelled the group booking in writing on 1 March 2002, but Payless Travel failed to warn Baba Krupa or obtain reliable written reinstatement.
Thirty-four passengers were refused boarding; Baba Krupa incurred hotel and replacement ticket costs totalling about £10,259.
The county court recorder found breach of the implied duty of reasonable care and skill and awarded damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Birmingham County Court judgment on a Part 20 counterclaim in travel agency proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on causation; Payless Travel remained liable for the damages awarded below.
enrichment.ratio: Once Balkan had threatened cancellation, a travel agent acting under section 13 of the 1982 Act owed a continuing duty to warn the principal and obtain clear confirmation of the booking; failure to do so was an effective cause of the principal's foreseeable replacement-travel losses even if Balkan's cancellation was also a cause.
legal_issues: Whether Payless Travel's duty ended on issue of tickets
Whether failure to warn of cancellation and to secure reinstatement breached section 13

enrichment.short_title: Nationwide organ retention group litigation lead claims
key_facts: Three lead claims in the Nationwide Organ Group Litigation concerned children's organs removed and retained after post-mortems without parents' knowledge at hospitals outside Alder Hey.
Parents claimed psychiatric injury, negligence, wrongful interference with a body, and human rights breaches following disclosure of organ retention practices.
The cases involved two hospital post-mortems (Harris and Shorter) and one coroner's post-mortem (Carpenter).
The trial was intended to resolve most of about 2,140 claims on the group register.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Lead trial and preliminary issues in group litigation following Bristol and Alder Hey organ retention disclosures.
enrichment.outcome: No tort of wrongful interference recognised in these circumstances; Mrs Shorter's negligence claim succeeded (£2,750), but Harris and Carpenter negligence claims failed on foreseeability; wrongful interference claims failed in all three lead cases.
enrichment.ratio: Parents have no possessory right in organs lawfully removed during an authorised post-mortem once the Doodeward exception applies, so wrongful interference claims fail; clinicians obtaining hospital post-mortem consent owe a duty to explain possible organ retention, but psychiatric injury must still be reasonably foreseeable, with primary victims judged by ordinary tort foreseeability.
legal_issues: Whether English law recognises a tort of wrongful interference with a body
Whether hospitals acquired lawful possession of retained organs under the Doodeward exception

enrichment.short_title: Validity of conditional fee agreement with contingent uplift
key_facts: Benaim and DMD settled an A13 road design negligence arbitration with Benaim ordered to pay DMD's costs.
DMD's solicitors acted under a CFA dated 31 August 2000 with a success uplift varying by amount recovered, capped at 25% of recovery.
Benaim argued the CFA was unenforceable for unlawful champerty despite complying with section 58.
An arbitrator upheld the CFA and amended his award after Benaim sought permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court appeal on the validity of a costs CFA following an arbitration costs award.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the CFA was valid and enforceable, and Benaim remained liable for DMD's costs under it.
enrichment.ratio: Section 58 renders enforceable conditional fee agreements that satisfy its conditions, and a CFA with a success uplift linked in part to amount recovered does not contain an independent champertous element if it remains within the statutory uplift cap and regulatory requirements.
legal_issues: Whether section 58 excludes further public-policy unenforceability for champerty

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe conviction where learning disability undiscovered at trial
key_facts: Darren Cash was convicted by a 10:2 majority at retrial of rape by aiding and abetting and kidnapping Deborah Ben-David after a pub encounter with his cousin Michael Cash.
Post-conviction psychological assessment revealed a full-scale IQ of 53, placing him in the lowest 0.1% of the population with mild mental retardation.
At trial he had not conducted a cut-throat defence against Michael Cash because counsel was unaware of his disability and followed his instructions.
Fresh evidence suggested he was suggestible, vulnerable under cross-examination, and should have had an appropriate adult at interview.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal with fresh evidence on mental capacity under section 23 of the 1968 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions on both counts quashed as unsafe and no retrial ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where the appellant's severe learning disability was unknown at trial and fresh expert evidence shows he lacked capacity fairly to comprehend proceedings or resist a dominant co-defendant's account, the conviction is unsafe even if the jury accepted the complainant's account of the underlying events.
legal_issues: Admissibility of fresh psychiatric evidence under section 23
Effect of undiagnosed learning disability on fitness to plead and trial fairness
Whether a different cut-throat defence would likely have affected the verdict
Appropriateness of retrial after long custody in unsuitable conditions

enrichment.short_title: Towage contract agency: owner not bound by Towcon terms
key_facts: Marine Blast chartered the dredger Von Rocks from Noas and entered into a Towcon towage contract with Targe for towage from Sweden to Scotland.
The tow failed and the dredger became a constructive total loss; Skandia as hull insurer settled a Swedish claim against Targe for SEK 1.1 million.
Targe claimed indemnity from Marine Blast under clause 18(2) of the Towcon contract, arguing Noas was not a party and therefore a third party.
Marine Blast contended Noas was bound through implied authority and clause 22 warranty of authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issues on whether Noas was a party to the towage contract and whether Targe could maintain its indemnity claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Noas was not a party to the towage contract and Targe's indemnity claim against Marine Blast could proceed on that basis.
enrichment.ratio: Implied authority to bind an owner to Towcon terms requires objective consent inferred from conduct; faxing Towcon documents without presenting them as terms binding the owner, especially in illegible form and without drawing attention to clause 22, is insufficient to make Noas a party or to authorise Marine Blast to contract on its behalf.
legal_issues: Whether Noas was a party to the towage contract through implied or apparent authority
Construction of Towcon clause 22 warranty of authority

Whether bailment-on-terms analogy could bind Noas without agency

enrichment.short_title: Construction Industry Scheme certificate compliance test
key_facts: JDC Services applied for a Construction Industry Scheme certificate but was refused because of late PAYE, CIS and corporation tax payments and late returns over the qualifying three-year period.
The Rochford General Commissioners allowed JDC's appeal despite finding the failures were not minor and technical, relying on the company's efforts to regularise its tax affairs.
The Revenue appealed by case stated on the construction of section 565 and the commissioners' jurisdiction.
JDC had previously been granted a certificate while in substantial tax arrears.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated from General Commissioners allowing a CIS certificate appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Revenue appeal allowed; the commissioners' decision was wrong in law and the CIS certificate was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Section 565(4) requires past tax failures to be both minor and technical and not to give reason to doubt future compliance; the commissioners had full appellate jurisdiction to review the Revenue's refusal but misapplied the statutory test and could not treat serious repeated lateness as satisfying section 565(3).
legal_issues: Whether section 565(4) imposes separate minor-and-technical and no-reason-to-doubt requirements
Whether commissioners may substitute their judgment on CIS certificate entitlement
Whether JDC's compliance history satisfied section 565(8)
Whether the High Court may quash a CIS certificate on case stated
